v.q: Which clue in a problem most strongly suggests the sliding window pattern?
o: The longest contiguous substring or subarray that satisfies a condition
Count the number of ways to climb a staircase
Find the shortest path in a weighted graph
Generate every permutation of the input
v.w: A window over contiguous elements is updated incrementally as it slides, so one pass is enough.

v.q: Which problem is NOT a natural fit for the sliding window pattern?
o: Count the ways to climb a staircase
Longest substring without repeating characters
Maximum sum of k consecutive elements
Smallest subarray with sum at least a target
v.w: Counting ways is a dynamic programming problem. Windows work on contiguous ranges that grow and shrink in one pass.

v.q: How does a hash map reduce two sum from O(n²) to O(n)?
o: It remembers values already seen, so each complement lookup takes O(1)
It sorts the array first and then compares the ends
It tries every pair but stops at the first match
It stores the array in reverse order
v.w: For each number you look up target minus the number in the map. It costs O(n) extra memory.

v.q: Find the first non-repeating character in a string in O(n). Which structure helps most?
o: A hash map of counts
A sorted copy of the string
A binary search tree of characters
A stack of characters
v.w: One pass counts each character and a second pass finds the first with count one. Both are O(n).

v.q: Which condition makes the two-pointers technique work on a pair-sum problem?
o: The array is sorted, so each sum shows which way to move
The array contains only positive integers and no zeros
The array length is a power of two or one less
The target value appears at least twice in the array
v.w: If the sum is too big the right pointer moves left, and if too small the left pointer moves right, discarding values that cannot work.

v.q: Which input makes two pointers NOT work directly for a pair-sum problem?
o: An unsorted array
A sorted array
A sorted array with duplicates
A sorted array of negative numbers
v.w: Moving a pointer relies on order. Sort first, or use a hash map when the original positions matter.

v.q: What do prefix sums let you do after one pass over the array?
o: Answer any range-sum query in O(1)
Sort the array in O(1)
Find the median without reading the data
Remove duplicates in place
v.w: The sum of positions i to j is prefix[j+1] - prefix[i], a difference of two precomputed values.

v.q: After building prefix sums, how long does the sum of elements 2 to 5 take?
o: O(1), one subtraction
O(n), a loop over the range
O(log n), a binary search
O(n log n), a sort first
v.w: prefix[6] - prefix[2] gives the range sum with two lookups.

v.q: Which two properties usually signal a dynamic programming problem?
o: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Sorted input and unique keys
A graph with no cycles and positive weights
A fixed window size and a string input
v.w: The same smaller problems repeat, and the best answer is built from best answers of smaller problems, so each can be computed once and reused.

v.q: Which problem is NOT a good fit for dynamic programming?
o: Find the shortest path in an unweighted graph
Longest common subsequence of two strings
Minimum number of coins for an amount
Number of paths in a grid
v.w: Breadth-first search solves the shortest unweighted path. The others have overlapping subproblems.

v.q: In backtracking, why do you remove the last choice after the recursive call returns?
o: To undo the choice so the next option starts from the same state
To free memory held by the recursion stack
To mark the choice as visited for ever
To sort the remaining choices
v.w: Choose, explore, undo is the core of backtracking. Without the undo, choices would leak into later branches.

v.q: Generating all subsets of an array is a classic use of which pattern?
o: Backtracking
Sliding window
Binary search
Prefix sums
v.w: For each element you choose it or skip it, explore, then undo the choice. That is the choose, explore, undo loop.

v.q: Why does greedy coin change fail for coins 1, 3 and 4 and amount 6?
o: Taking the largest coin first gives 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 needs only 2
The amount 6 can never be made from those coins
Greedy always fails when the coins include 1
Dynamic programming also gives 3 coins
v.w: A locally best choice is not always globally best. Dynamic programming tries all coins for each amount and finds 2.

v.q: Which statement about greedy algorithms is NOT true?
o: A greedy choice always gives the global optimum
It is fast, usually O(n log n) after sorting
Interval scheduling can be solved greedily
It can fail where dynamic programming succeeds
v.w: Greedy is only correct when a local choice is provably safe. The coin change example 1, 3, 4 shows it can fail.

v.q: What should you do first when given a coding problem in an interview?
o: Clarify the requirements and constraints and work a small example
Start writing the optimised solution at once
Memorise the closest known problem and recite its answer
Ask to skip to the next question
v.w: Clarifying inputs, size limits and edge cases avoids solving the wrong problem and often reveals the pattern.

v.q: Which habit most reduces wrong answers in a coding interview?
o: Test your code on a small example and an edge case
Start coding without asking questions
Choose the first approach you think of
Skip complexity analysis
v.w: Walking through a small input and edge cases such as empty or single-element catches bugs before the interviewer does.
